The odds of Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) merging sometime next year have been growing. Prediction market odds jumped earlier this month after Elon Musk's biographer, Walter Isaacson, told CNBC he was confident a merger is coming, since keeping the companies separate makes no sense. This was followed by the two companies picking board members to begin official merger talks.

Isaacson's comments raised the odds that SpaceX would announce a merger with Tesla before March 1, 2027, from 27% on Nov. 11, 2026, to 62% two days later. They now sit at 67%, as of Nov. 24 on Kalshi. Meanwhile, the odds of a merger announcement before the end of 2027 are at 89% on Polymarket.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Now, a merger isn't a foregone conclusion and does face some hurdles, but it does seem very likely at this point. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections complicate matters a bit, as Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson told Bloomberg that a potential merger would face "tremendous scrutiny." Meanwhile, more than half of all Tesla shareholders would need to vote to approve the merger, not just those who decide to vote. Musk owns nearly 20% of the company, but Tesla also has a significant retail shareholder base that would have to vote on the deal for it to pass.

Despite these obstacles, there is still a very good shot that the companies announce a merger next year and complete it by the end of 2028. In such a scenario, it would be best to purchase shares of Tesla, the acquired company. With a little over $5,000, an investor could buy around 13 shares of Tesla.

A synergistic acquisition

An acquisition of Tesla by SpaceX ultimately makes a lot of sense. First, it unites Musk's two largest companies and will allow him to focus on a single vision instead of splitting his time between the two. Second, the companies already have an important joint venture in the form of their massive chip manufacturing facility, Terafab, so it would make sense to have this under one roof. Finally, the companies' businesses complement each other.

More than anything, both SpaceX and Tesla are about the future, and together they give Musk and investors more shots on goal. Meanwhile, SpaceX could ultimately need some of Tesla's technology to build its planned data centers in space, including solar and Optimus robots. As such, the deal makes sense from a synergy perspective, and the company would be able to cut some overlapping corporate costs.

Brad Gerstner's Altimeter Capital opened a new position of 1,915,440 shares in Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) during the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026. The stake was worth $680 million at quarter-end, according to the 13F filed Nov. 16.

24/7 Wall St.

The same filing shows full exits from Qualcomm (NASDAQ:QCOM) and Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT). Taken together, the moves show a fund pulling money out of chip hardware and putting it into Tesla's autonomy and robotics plans.

TSLA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
A Rotation Out of Chips and Into Tesla

Tesla made up 6.94% of Altimeter's $9.8 billion in reported long positions, which are spread across just 16 stocks. NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) is still the largest disclosed holding. Altimeter also sold all of its shares in two more chip-equipment suppliers and opened a put position on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH).

A put gains value when the underlying asset falls, so it works as a bearish hedge. A 13F does not show its cost, strike, or expiration, and the put is excluded from the long total.

Tesla Data Behind the Thesis

Gerstner has not explained the trade publicly. Tesla's third-quarter results point to an AI and autonomy story. The company launched Cybercab into its unsupervised Robotaxi fleet in Austin on Sept. 3, and cumulative unsupervised miles rose 8x from the prior quarter to about 2M. Active FSD subscriptions reached 1.74M, up from 1.04M a year earlier.

Space Exploration Technologies has seen momentum cool in recent weeks, with the share price down 11.2% over the last seven sessions and 21.8% year to date, as merger headlines, heavy AI chip financing, and shifting ETF flows reset expectations around both growth potential and balance sheet risk.

Space Exploration Technologies now trades at a steep discount to both analyst targets and some intrinsic value models after its recent slide. Is that gap compensating you for AI chip leverage, merger risk, and governance questions, or is it mispricing them?

Most Popular Narrative: 39% Undervalued

The latest community narrative pegs Space Exploration Technologies at a fair value of $207 per share, compared with the last close at $125.81, and frames that gap through a very specific view on growth, capital intensity, and segment mix. According to deyan_89mg6, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the key question is how this vertically integrated platform converts that growth into durable per share economics.

SpaceX should no longer be viewed primarily as a launch company. Its emerging structure is more appropriately analyzed as a vertically integrated infrastructure platform built around Space, Connectivity, and AI. The investment case therefore depends less on launch revenue alone and increasingly on the interaction between Starship, Starlink, Starlink Mobile, AI compute, software, and semiconductor infrastructure.

That framework matters if you are weighing Tesla stock as a merger vehicle into SPCX. The narrative assumes a discount rate of 7.236% and treats Space Exploration Technologies as an infrastructure platform spanning rockets, broadband and AI compute rather than a single segment telecom stock.

On those assumptions, the fair value of $207 sits well above both Space Exploration Technologies' recent share price and the merger chatter that has pulled focus back to leverage, cash runway and dilution. Revenue of $32,043.0m, an annual top line growth rate of 83.1%, and forecast revenue growth of 51.2% per year are all plugged into a story where future profitability and return on equity are expected to improve, but are not yet reflected in current earnings because the group remains loss making today with net income of $3,431.0m in the red.

Apple (NasdaqGS:AAPL) is challenging the trading of tokenized versions of its shares on newly expanded blockchain-based markets.

Crypto exchange OKX and the New York Stock Exchange parent have launched a 24/7 tokenized U.S. securities venue that includes Apple, Nvidia, and Tesla.

Apple and other issuers are raising questions over control of their equity's digital representation, shareholder rights, and regulatory oversight.

The clash over 24/7 tokenized Apple shares trading comes alongside broader shifts in how traditional stocks intersect with blockchain markets. We have also flagged 1 warning sign for Apple.

NasdaqGS:AAPL 1-Year Stock Price Chart

Apple is a US tech giant with a US$5.1b market cap that earns most of its influence from the iPhone, Mac, iPad, and a growing mix of wearables and accessories, so any move to tokenize its equity touches one of the most widely held consumer-tech platforms on the planet. Because its products underpin large parts of the digital ecosystem, questions over how Apple shares appear on blockchain venues go straight to how traditional blue-chip ownership might be represented in newer trading pipes.

See how Apple's balance sheet measures up.

Why does Apple care if its shares trade as tokens on a blockchain?

Control is the first issue. Apple is pushing back because tokenized versions of its equity can create parallel trading channels that sit outside its direct oversight, raising questions about who is responsible for accurate corporate actions, shareholder communication, and how those digital claims tie back to real securities on regulated venues.

Does this clash change the current Apple Narrative for investors?

The dispute mainly stresses the legal and regulatory overhang that the current Apple Narrative already highlights as a constraint on upside. It adds another wrinkle alongside existing cases, while the core story still hangs on Apple keeping demand strong for higher priced, AI capable devices without letting margin pressure from costs and compliance squeeze profitability too far.

See how these catalysts shape Apple's path to a $339 fair value.

What is the key number or milestone to watch from here?

The practical marker is how much 24/7 tokenized trading develops compared with Apple's regular volume on primary exchanges, once the new venue scales its planned 113 assets. If parallel activity becomes material relative to standard turnover, regulators and Apple could both step up pressure, which would shape how this experiment settles.

title: Ford Motor vs. Tesla: Which Automaker Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Ford Motor vs. Tesla: Which Automaker Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Brendan Coffey, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 12:13 PM CST 6 min read
F
TSLA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The battle for automotive dominance pits century-old manufacturing scale against high-tech electric innovation. Choosing between Ford Motor Company (NYSE:F) and Tesla Inc. (NASDAQ:TSLA) requires weighing established commercial strength against aggressive future-focused growth.

Ford relies on its dominant position in trucks and commercial fleets to fund its transition to electric vehicles. Tesla continues to lead the global market for electric vehicles while expanding into energy storage and artificial intelligence. These two companies represent very different philosophies on how vehicles should be built, sold, and powered for the next decade.

The case for Ford Motor

Ford Motor generates revenue by selling trucks, SUVs, and commercial vans through segments like Ford Pro and Ford Blue. It serves global retail, commercial, and government customers. This business is supported by a network of over 8,200 independently owned dealerships worldwide.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $187 billion. This represented a revenue decline of roughly 1.4% compared to the prior twelve-month period. During this same time frame, the company reported a net loss of about $7.8 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly -4.2%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Ford Motor reported a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 4.7x, a measure of total debt divided by shareholder equity. Its current ratio, measuring the ability to pay short-term bills, was roughly 1.1x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was approximately $12.5 billion.

The case for Tesla

Tesla operates a vertically integrated business model focusing on electric vehicles and sustainable energy products. The company sells vehicles directly to consumers and provides energy storage to residential, commercial, and utility customers. These operations span major markets across North America, Europe, and Asia.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue was about $103.6 billion. This reflects a revenue growth of approximately 8.3%. The company also reported net income of about $3.2 billion during this period, resulting in a net margin of approximately 3.1%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, Tesla maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.1x, which indicates its total debt is very low relative to its shareholder equity. The current ratio, a measure of how easily a company can cover immediate bills, was close to 2.2x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, the company generated about $6.2 billion in free cash flow.

Space stocks are moving in different directions. AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) is posting the group's sharpest reversal while the broader market sells off. AST SpaceMobile stock is at $25.78, up 9% in afternoon trading. Earlier in the session, the stock traded down 4% at $22.73.

3DSculptor / iStock via Getty Images

The rebound starts from a heavily sold base. Even after the jump, AST SpaceMobile stock is down 65% year to date (YTD), so most of the year's losses are still on the books. The best-supported explanation is dip buying in a beaten-down stock, with buyers stepping in once the early selling faded.

Recent Setbacks That Left AST SpaceMobile Oversold

AST SpaceMobile has taken a series of hits this month. On November 9, the company disclosed Q3 2026 revenue of $42.32 million, up 187.1% year over year (YoY) but missing the $46 million consensus. Management held its full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $150 million to $200 million and ended the quarter with $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents. The company's net loss reached $132.38 million, which included $52.34 million in stock-based compensation.

ASTS Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.

Sentiment has swung both ways since then. Jim Cramer called AST SpaceMobile "a very hard stock to own" on November 18. B. Riley upgraded the stock on November 19 with a $48 price target, arguing that launch and funding risks are "already priced in."
